chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Ismail al-Jawhari, from Abu Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
If I were to perform a Hajj, it would be more beloved to me than if I were to free a neck (slave), and a neck — until it reached ten, and similar to it, and similar to it, until it reached seventy.

And if I were to support a household from the Muslims, satisfying their hunger, clothing their nakedness, and restraining their faces from (begging of) the people, it would be more beloved to me than if I were to perform a Hajj, and a Hajj, and a Hajj — until it reached ten, and ten, and ten, and similar to it, and similar to it, until it reached seventy.

key_terms.أَهْلَ بَيْتٍ: a household / family unit (here referring to a poor Muslim family, not the Prophet's family)
key_terms.عَوْرَتَهُمْ: their nakedness / private parts (clothe what must be covered — basic dignified clothing)
key_terms.وُجُوهَهُمْ: their faces (to restrain their faces from the people = to spare them from having to beg)

ai.seo_question: Is supporting a poor Muslim family better than performing hajj according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) establishes a three-way hierarchy of merit: performing hajj surpasses freeing up to seventy slaves, yet supporting an entire Muslim household — feeding them, clothing them, and preserving their dignity from begging — surpasses even seventy pilgrimages. The teaching reflects the Imam's emphasis on active social welfare as a higher-priority obligation than individual acts of worship and personal merit-seeking. In the context of early Islamic society where manumission was a major charity act and slavery was widespread, this ranking would have been striking to the original audience, underscoring that collective human dignity and basic needs take precedence.
